column1: What is the core architectural invariant of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)?
column2: The generation distribution is conditioned on both a parametric model distribution and a non-parametric document store that can be updated independently of the model weights, decoupling knowledge storage from language generation.

column1: What is the formal equation for RAG's output probability P(y|q)?
column2: P(y|q) = Σ_{d∈top-k(D,q)} P(d|q) · P(y|q,d) — a sum over retrieved documents of the retrieval probability times the generator's conditional probability given query and document.

column1: What are the three structural failure modes of purely parametric LLM knowledge that RAG addresses?
column2: 1) Knowledge cutoff/temporal staleness, 2) Hallucination under distribution shift (confabulation on underrepresented topics), 3) Unverifiable provenance (no ability to cite sources).

column1: What is the difference between RAG-Sequence and RAG-Token as defined by Lewis et al. (2020)?
column2: RAG-Sequence conditions the entire output sequence on the same single retrieved document. RAG-Token allows each output token to be conditioned on a potentially different retrieved document within one generation pass.

column1: Why does hallucination occur under distribution shift according to the maximum-likelihood estimator view of LLMs?
column2: It is expected behavior, not a bug: when queries touch domains underrepresented in training data, the model fills gaps with statistically plausible but factually wrong tokens because it is interpolating beyond its training support.

column1: What is the Information Bottleneck objective that formalizes ideal contextual compression in RAG?
column2: min_C [ -I(T;Y) + β·I(T;X) ], where T=C(X) is the compressed context, Y is the ground-truth answer, and β controls the tradeoff between relevance (predicting Y) and compactness (minimizing retained info from X).

column1: What is the key invariant that compression techniques must preserve to avoid 'over-compression' failures?
column2: I(C(X); Y) ≈ I(X; Y) — the mutual information between the compressed context and the answer must approximate the mutual information between the original context and the answer; violations cause hallucinated facts, dropped entities, and broken reasoning chains.

column1: Why must contextual compression operate under a strict latency budget in production RAG systems?
column2: Compression must be faster than retrieval latency plus generation latency combined, or it adds net overhead to end-to-end query time; this typically binds compression to sub-100ms wall-clock budgets, ruling out multi-pass neural re-ranking as a sole strategy.

column1: What is the architectural distinction between Fusion-in-Decoder (FiD) and naive prompt stuffing in RAG generation?
column2: FiD independently encodes each retrieved passage and lets the decoder attend over concatenated encoder states, avoiding the O(k·l) attention cost that naive prompt stuffing pays by concatenating all passages directly in the prompt.

column1: Why can't cross-encoder models be used as first-stage retrievers in RAG, despite often being more accurate rerankers?
column2: Cross-encoders score query-document pairs jointly and cannot pre-index documents independently; this makes them O(N) at query time (must score every document), making them computationally unsuitable as first-stage retrievers over large corpora.

column1: What is the anisotropy problem in transformer embedding spaces, and why does it matter for RAG retrieval?
column2: Raw transformer embeddings cluster in a narrow cone of the embedding space rather than being uniformly distributed (isotropic), compressing the effective capacity of the vector index. Post-hoc whitening or contrastive fine-tuning corrects this to improve retrieval quality.

column1: Why is naively stuffing an entire document corpus into an LLM's context window economically and computationally infeasible, even with large context windows?
column2: A corpus of 10,000 documents at 2,000 tokens each would require 20 million tokens per query; this is prohibitive both in cost and because attention complexity scales as O(n²) in sequence length, motivating chunking plus retrieval instead.
